hints: Start by picturing what has to happen for a reaction without an enzyme - particles must collide with enough energy to break existing bonds. What could an enzyme change about that hurdle?
Now focus on the active site - how does holding substrates together in the right position and interacting with their bonds and charges make breaking and forming bonds easier?
walkthrough:
Remember What Activation Energy Means**
Activation energy is the energy needed to break bonds in reactants so new bonds can form. Without help, only collisions with a lot of energy succeed. Enzymes do not add energy, they lower the hurdle by offering a different route.

How The Active Site Lowers The Hurdle**
You form an enzyme-substrate complex. The active site holds substrates close together and in the correct orientation, puts strain on key bonds, and R groups can transfer charges or chemical groups. That means bonds break and form more easily, so less energy is needed to reach the transition state.

Final answer: Enzymes provide an alternative pathway of lower activation energy by forming an enzyme-substrate complex. They bring reactants close together in the active site in the correct orientation and put strain on bonds / transfer charges or groups so bonds break and form more easily.

hints: Look at each curve separately first - as you move right along the time axis, what happens to concentration of PABA for every inhibitor line?
Now compare top to bottom at the same time - what is the order of the curves from no inhibitor down to 30 microM, and what does that tell you about rate?
Zoom in on the very start of the graph around 0 to 10-20 min - do the lines start apart or together?
Pick two fixed times to quote numbers, for example 60 min for no inhibitor versus 30 microM, and 40 min for 3 microM versus 10 microM, to support each trend.
walkthrough:
Overall Time Trend**
All five curves rise to the right. That means product accumulates with time. The curves also flatten slightly after about 40-50 min, so rate slows as substrate is used up, but the main point is concentration of PABA increases with time.

Inhibitor Effect - Compare Like With Like**
Fix the time and read vertically. Higher inhibitor always sits lower. No inhibitor is highest, then 1 microM, then 3 microM, then 10 microM, then 30 microM lowest. So increasing inhibitor decreases PABA formed and slows the reaction. The gap between 0 and 1 microM is small, the gap between 1 and 3 microM and higher is much larger.

Early Similarity And Data Support**
Early on the curves overlap. Up to about 10-20 min all give ~0.7-2.0 microM, showing same initial rate. Then they separate. Always quote values with units to earn credit: for example at 60 min ~4.5 microM with no inhibitor, ~4.2 microM with 1 microM, ~3.0 microM with 3 microM, ~2.1 microM with 10 microM and ~1.3 microM with 30 microM.

Final answer: As time increases, concentration of PABA produced increases for all inhibitor concentrations. Increasing inhibitor concentration decreases concentration of PABA / slows rate of reaction. At the start, e.g. 0 to ~10-20 min, there is little / no difference between curves. E.g. at 60 min no inhibitor gives ~4.5 microM PABA while 30 microM inhibitor gives ~1.3 microM; at 40 min 3 microM gives ~2.5 microM while 10 microM gives ~1.7 microM.

hints: Think about what distinguishes the two types - one can be out-competed by adding more substrate, the other cannot. What variable must you therefore change systematically?
To make it a fair test, what must you keep the same and what two conditions must you run side by side?
How will you tell which type it is from the results - think about rate at high substrate or Km and Vmax on a rate graph?
walkthrough:
Vary Substrate To Test Competition**
A competitive inhibitor binds the active site, so lots of substrate can out-compete it. A non-competitive inhibitor binds elsewhere, so extra substrate cannot overcome it. So you need a series of tubes with different substrate concentrations, from very low to very high.

Run With And Without Inhibitor As Fair Test**
Repeat the whole series with inhibitor present at one fixed concentration and without inhibitor as control. Keep everything else constant - same enzyme concentration, same temperature, same pH, same time for measurement. Measure initial rate of PABA formation.

Interpret Km And Vmax**
Plot rate against substrate concentration. If high substrate restores the rate to the control maximum, it is competitive: Km is increased but Vmax is unchanged. If Vmax stays lower even at high substrate, it is non-competitive: Vmax decreased, Km unchanged.

Final answer: Carry out reaction at a range of substrate concentrations (at least 5, including low and high) both with and without a fixed concentration of inhibitor, keeping enzyme concentration, temperature, pH and other variables constant. Measure initial rate / PABA formed. If increasing substrate overcomes inhibition, inhibitor is competitive (increased Km, same Vmax); if not, it is non-competitive (same Km, decreased Vmax).

hints: Compare the two cells - humans can take ready-made folic acid from diet and lack the PABA enzyme, while bacteria must make it. What happens to bacteria if that making step is blocked?
walkthrough:
Why It Kills Bacteria But Not You**
Bacteria cannot absorb folic acid through their walls, they must make PABA to make folic acid for growth. Block the enzyme and they starve of folic acid and stop growing. Human cells simply take folic acid from food and do not even have this enzyme, so the inhibitor targets only bacterial cells and does not harm human cells.

Final answer: Bacteria cannot make / make less folic acid so cannot grow / reproduce and die, while human cells are unaffected as they absorb folic acid from diet and do not have the enzyme to make PABA.

hints: List what antibiotics usually attack in bacteria - walls, membranes, ribosomes, enzymes and growing metabolism. Which of these does a virus have on its own?
Think about where a virus spends most of its life cycle - why would that location make it hard for a drug to reach without harming the host?
walkthrough:
No Bacterial Targets To Hit**
Antibiotics work on living, growing bacterial cells by hitting walls, membranes, ribosomes or metabolic enzymes. A virus particle is just nucleic acid in a protein coat, sometimes with an envelope. It has no wall, no ribosomes, few or no enzymes and no metabolism of its own.

Hidden Inside Host Cells**
Viruses replicate inside human host cells, so a drug cannot reach them without entering our own cells and risking harm. That is why there are few effective antiviral drugs compared to antibacterial drugs.

Final answer: Viruses have few targets as they have no cell wall / membrane / ribosomes and have no / few enzymes and no metabolism / growth of their own. They are inside host cells out of reach, and antibiotics do not act on protein capsid / viral envelope.

hints: Resistance spreads when bacteria are exposed to antibiotics unnecessarily - when should antibiotics not be used at all?
When they must be used, what rules about choice, dose, completing the course and prescription control reduce survival of resistant mutants?
walkthrough:
Avoid Unnecessary Selection Pressure**
Every unnecessary exposure selects for resistant mutants. So do not prescribe for viral infections or as preventative medicine, and only use when necessary after testing which antibiotic works. Use a narrow-spectrum drug when the pathogen is known.

Use Correctly And Contain Spread**
Ensure correct dose and that patients complete the full course and do not share leftovers, with supply on prescription only. Other valid steps are combining or rotating antibiotics, keeping some as last resort, reducing farm use, and breaking transmission by hygiene, quarantine and vaccination.

Final answer: Any two: do not use for viral infections / do not use as preventative; use only when necessary with correct effective antibiotic, e.g. after sensitivity test, narrow spectrum if pathogen known; ensure correct dose and complete full course, do not use leftover / other people's antibiotics, supply on prescription only; rotate / combine antibiotics, keep some as last resort, reduce agricultural use; improve hygiene / vaccination to break transmission.
